title: GNSS-disciplined clock holdover per oscillator grade, and a slow time-walk spoof
summary: A stdlib-only simulation of a GNSS-disciplined oscillator (type-2 PLL on a noisy 1PPS) for TCXO, OCXO, rubidium and chip-scale atomic clock grades, with ADEV, aging and temperature figures taken from Vig's oscillator comparison table and the Microchip SA65 datasheet. It reports time error after 1 min to 24 h of GNSS outage (Monte Carlo median and 95th percentile, next to an analytic estimate), then walks GNSS time off slowly and compares an internal steering-plausibility monitor with a cross-check against a second time source, including a guard that drops into holdover on alarm and no-spoof control runs.
verified: ran with python3.14.7 stdlib on 2026-11-06 (default arguments, about 5 s); output pasted verbatim in README. 9 unittest tests pass, including an ADEV check of the noise model, a no-spoof negative control and a planted blind-detector control that proves the cross-source alarm can fail. Oscillator parameters are datasheet/table values; PPS noise, second-source noise/asymmetry, temperature fraction and detector thresholds are stated assumptions. No hardware or real GNSS data was used, and none of the related repos was run.
shows: GNSS-disciplined oscillator sim (TCXO / CSAC / OCXO / Rb): holdover error after outage, slow time-walk spoof vs internal and cross-source monitors
key_result: [24 h holdover](README.md#output-ran-on-2026-11-06-python-3147-default-arguments-about-5-s), median: TCXO 59.58 us, CSAC 1.27 us, OCXO 610.0 ns, Rb 43.8 ns (no temperature term)

title: Network of GNSS-disciplined clocks: holdover from peers, spoof isolation by cross-node consistency, ADEV-weighted ensemble
summary: A stdlib-only simulation of six GNSS-disciplined sites (TCXO, OCXO, CSAC, Rb oscillators imported from timing-holdover) linked by PTP-like two-way time transfer with static path asymmetry, exponential queueing delay and a lucky-packet filter. Three scenarios: regional jamming where GNSS-less nodes hold time from peers vs alone; a 1-50 ns/s time push on one node caught by a least-squares cross-node consistency check that isolates it before GNSS-denied nodes take its time; and all GNSS lost, comparing every node alone, following the best clock, and an Allan-deviation-weighted paper-clock ensemble. Reports time error per node, time under 1 / 1.5 / 5 / 10 us budgets (G.8271 levels), detection time, false alarms, and how much uncalibrated or changed path asymmetry costs (A/2). A separate real-data mode (fetch_data.py + real_link.py) characterises PTP over private 5G SA, public 5G NSA and 4G from the open Kalnins dataset (Zenodo 14230741: PPS-vs-PPS truth, PTPd logs, a UPF packet capture) and replays the measured time error into the jamming and spoof scenarios.
verified: Synthetic: ran with python3.14.7 stdlib on 2026-11-06, default arguments, 51 s; output pasted verbatim in README (plus a --temp-fraction 0 run of scenario c). Real-data mode: fetch_data.py downloaded the Zenodo 14230741 zip (MD5 945aefa3013bc926d748f7e820275069 matched the record) and real_link.py ran on it in 19 s, output pasted verbatim. 21 unittest tests pass under plain /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 (3.14.7) in about 4 s with the data, 18 pass and 3 skip without it; they include parser tests on inline fixtures (PPS, PTPd with glued rows, a hand-built pcapng), a same-seed check that an added 2 us asymmetry moves time by exactly 1 us, a check that a replayed constant 2 us link error becomes 2 us of relay time error, a no-spoof control and a planted blind-detector control. Oscillator parameters are the parent's datasheet/table values; synthetic network delays, asymmetries, PPS noise, temperature fraction, site layout and thresholds are stated assumptions. Real data: PPS truth and PTPd logs come from different runs and PTP software (Timebeat vs PTPd), each record is 15 min and is looped for the replay. None of the related repos was run.
shows: Six GNSS-disciplined sites over PTP-like links: holdover from peers vs alone under regional jamming, cross-node consistency check isolating a time push, ADEV-weighted ensemble vs best clock, cost of path asymmetry
runtime: ~50 s synthetic (spoof study alone ~10 s); real-data mode ~20 s after a 60 MB download
key_result: [Synthetic network, 10 seeds](README.md#output-ran-on-2026-11-06-python-3147-default-arguments-51-s): jammed TCXO alone exceeds 1.5 us after 16-22 min, from peers stays under 1 us for 24 h; 50 ns/s push on the relay isolated in 50 s (5/5), downstream nodes 332 ns vs 360 us unguarded, 0 false alarms in 40 h; unknown asymmetry A costs A/2 (4 us => 2.16 us); all GNSS lost 24 h worst node: ensemble 1.13 us, best clock 2.27 us, alone 4.18 ms. [Real PTP over 5G, Zenodo 14230741](README.md#real-data-output-ran-2026-11-06-python-3147-default-arguments-19-s): PPS truth |TE| median 1.6-2.3 ms (private 5G SA) and 9.4 ms (public 5G NSA), at most 0.3 % of seconds under 1.5 us; implied asymmetry 3.3-4.7 ms (SA), 14.9 ms (NSA), about 10^4 x the sample's radio links; replayed into (a) the jammed relay stays at 1.6-2.4 ms for 24 h vs under 1 us on the synthetic links

title: Two independent absolute sources on one real flight: visual fixes + terrain-relative navigation with solution-separation integrity (VPAIR over NRW 1 m LiDAR)
summary: Adds terrain-relative navigation as a second absolute source to the real VPAIR flight (8.53 km after GNSS loss, Rhine valley between Bad Honnef and Koenigswinter, east of Bonn). VO and visual fixes are the cached real-imagery front end of e2e-visual-nav-vpair (imported, no GPU). TRN sensors are simulated from real terrain at the real VPAIR poses: a downward heightmap (scanning LiDAR / stereo stand-in) from the Geobasis NRW 1 m DSM matched by terrain-heightmap-pf's v2 particle filter against a 5 m NRW map or a Copernicus GLO-30 map, and a 40 deg radar altimeter (blind-flight-bench beam model, noise, dropouts) matched by batch TERCOM against the DSM's leading-edge beam map. Fusion and integrity reuse altpnt-integrity v2 (heading/scale EKF, chi-square gate, solution separation, protection level, per-source fault priors), with TRN R from the TRN's own no-truth sigma. Reports error, PL availability at AL 25/50/100 m, HMI/MI with each source alone vs both over 10 TRN seeds, and injects a visual map misregistration and a TRN ambiguity (secondary match peak), with the monitor order swapped as a control and a three-source variant.
verified: Ran 2026-11-06 on Apple M2 Max, CPython 3.12.14, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1, rasterio 1.5.2: fetch_terrain.py (46 NRW DOM1 tiles, GLO-30 window, 125 s), run_two_source.py with 10 TRN seeds (107 s), screenshot.sh at frames 130 and 198. Map stride 8 (360 m tiles), heading +2 deg, 188 frames after GNSS loss: VO + visual fixes alone 9.7 m RMS but solution-separation PL median 1.2 km (1.6 % available at AL 50); + LiDAR-heightmap TRN 2.6 m RMS, PL median 30.5 m, available 14.4 / 84.4 / 100 % at AL 25 / 50 / 100 m; GLO-30-map TRN 55.6 % at AL 100 only; radar-altimeter TERCOM 10.9 % at AL 100 with 6 false detections. 0 HMI in every fault-free run. Faults: misregistration and TRN ambiguity detected 10/10 with the LiDAR TRN, no HMI, but two-source attribution of the misregistration follows the monitor's source order (control: swapped order flips it), and the three-source variant mis-excludes and gives 19 HMI epochs at AL 50 under TRN ambiguity. Tests: venv 14 pass; plain python3 7 pass, 7 skip. Altimeter and heightmap are simulated from real terrain at real poses, not recorded; LiDAR map and sensor share one DSM.
group: Integrity and GNSS-loss response on a vehicle
shows: Second absolute source (TRN from real NRW LiDAR at real VPAIR poses) turns solution-separation integrity from 1.6 % to 84 % available at AL 50 m; fault injection with detection and attribution limits
runtime: fetch ~2 min (46 tiles, ~120 MB, git-ignored); run 107 s for 10 seeds on M2; needs the VPAIR sample (0.86 GB, shared with relative-nav-benchmark)
key_result: [VPAIR, 8.5 km, map stride 8](README.md#results): PL available at AL 50 m 1.6 % with visual fixes alone => 84.4 % with a LiDAR-heightmap TRN (PL median 1.2 km => 30.5 m), 0 HMI; GLO-30 TRN only helps at AL 100 (55.6 %), radar-altimeter TERCOM barely (10.9 %); [faults](README.md#fault-injection) detected 10/10, two-source attribution set by monitor order, three-source exclusion gives HMI

title: UGV GNSS outage on a real log: wheel odometry + IMU, innovation gate, drag detector
summary: Stdlib-only ground-vehicle loop on a real NCLT Segway session (2013-01-10, 1022 s, 1139 m, 42 MB download): consumer GPS at 1 Hz fused with MEMS strapdown INS (the 8-state EKF of gnss-ins-ekf-outage, imported), wheel speed + MEMS gyro, or wheel speed + KVH fibre-optic gyro. Measures dead-reckoning drift through injected 10/30/60/120 s outages and one real 39.6 s GNSS gap against NCLT SLAM truth, what a chi-square innovation gate does with real multipath, and detection time of an injected coherent drag (synthetic attack on real fixes) for the gate and an odometry-vs-GNSS displacement test, with false alarms on the clean log.
verified: Ran 2026-11-06 with /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 3.14.7, stdlib only (run with -I). fetch_nclt.py downloaded and sha256-verified groundtruth_2013-01-10.csv (20.7 MB) and 2013-01-10_sen.tar.gz (21.7 MB) from the NCLT S3 bucket in ~27 s; ugv_loop.py (all four reports, ~26 s) output saved in results/all-2013-01-10.txt and quoted in the README. Sensor conventions checked against truth (gyro z slope 0.994, KVH rate sign, wheel scale 1.07). 11 unittest tests pass with data, 7 pass + 4 skip without data; mutations (inert gate, zero drag) make the gate and drag tests fail. One session only; truth is NCLT SLAM which fuses the same wheel odometry; the drag is a position offset on recorded fixes, not an RF spoof. robot_localization, DRIFT and KF-GINS were not run.
group: Integrity and GNSS-loss response on a vehicle
shows: Real Segway log (NCLT): GNSS outages bridged by wheel odometry vs MEMS INS, chi-square gate on real multipath, injected drag detection with gate vs odometry displacement test
runtime: download 42 MB in ~30 s; all reports ~26 s; tests ~4 s
key_result: [Real NCLT log](README.md#results): 60 s outage drift median 57 m MEMS INS vs 3.9 m wheels + MEMS gyro vs 2.5 m wheels + FOG (120 s p95 34.5 / 16.7 m with wheels); gate rejected 16/40 multipath fixes and 0/800 good; injected 1 m/s drag caught by the odometry displacement test in 16-18 s (8/8), by the gate in 30-44 s; 0.1 m/s drag caught in at most 2 of 8 runs by either; 1 alarm per detector on the clean log, during a real 46-55 m multipath episode

title: USV own-ship navigation under GNSS spoofing: radar-to-chart fixes and an integrity monitor in the Oresund
summary: A simulated USV runs a 19.6 km transit over real geography (Lillgrund => Drogden channel => Copenhagen approach) built from OpenStreetMap coastline, Oresund bridge, wind turbines and seamarks, with 75 min of real Danish Maritime Authority AIS traffic as radar targets. Compass + bottom-track speed log dead reckoning, a 720-azimuth marine radar ray-cast with clutter, incidence-dependent detection and ship occlusion, likelihood-field + point-to-line ICP matching of returns to the chart (with degenerate, ambiguous and few-return checks), a 4-state EKF that also calibrates compass bias from matched heading, and a monitor (solution separation + 30 s GNSS-vs-radar/DR mean test, exclusion only when the GNSS-free filter has recent radar fixes). Over 5 seeds a slow GNSS drag (0.003 m/s^2 to 0.6 m/s) is excluded 125-131 s after onset near the coast at a 23-26 m offset (max error 10-25 m vs 1391-1395 m for GNSS+DR and for a single filter with radar but only innovation gates); onset in open water is caught at 202-250 s (max 71-102 m); a 1.5 km radar range makes it fail (175-1024 m). Zero false alarms in 25 runs. Writes navdash/1 JSONL for templates/demo-dashboard and own-ship CoT via the mavlink-to-tak-cot builder; README maps the pieces onto OpenCPN/radar_pi, Signal K, colav-simulator and MOOS-IvP.
verified: Ran 2026-11-06 on macOS with python 3.14.7 stdlib: 15 unit tests pass and three negative controls (detection off, degeneracy check off, isolation rule off) each make the targeted test fail; run.py for 5 scenarios x 4 configurations x 5 seeds, numbers in the README come from example_output/summary_5seeds.*; plot.py with matplotlib 3.11.2 (python 3.13.15); example_output/spoof-coastal loaded in templates/demo-dashboard in headless Chrome (metrics panel read). Fixtures built from Overpass (OSM) and a locally downloaded DMA AIS file for 2026-10-20. Not done: real radar data, S-57 ENC input, CoT in a TAK client, running any of the linked maritime stacks. Sensors, radar and attacks are simulated; the simulated world equals the OSM chart apart from buoy offsets, so radar fix errors are optimistic.
shows: USV own-ship nav in the Oresund: compass + speed-log DR, simulated radar matched to the real OSM chart, monitor excludes spoofed GNSS
key_result: [5 seeds](README.md#results-5-seeds-real-outputs): coastal drag excluded 125-131 s after onset, max error 10-25 m vs 1391-1395 m without the monitor; 0 false alarms in 25 runs

title: VIO to MAVLink bridge with ENU/FLU to NED/FRD conversion
summary: Sends an external pose source (VIO topic or CSV log) to PX4 EKF2 or ArduPilot EKF3 as VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE or ODOMETRY for GPS-denied position hold. The frame conversion (ENU/FLU to NED/FRD, world to body velocity, MAVLink covariance layout) is a stdlib module with unit tests, and the pymavlink sender plus small set_params / watch_ekf helpers sit on top.
verified: Ran on 2026-11-06: frames.py tests (8 OK) and --dry-run on python3.14.7; the pymavlink ODOMETRY path ran against ArduCopter 4.6.3 SITL (EKF3 'is using external nav data', flags 0x033f) and PX4 v1.17.0 SIH (estimator_status_flags cs_ev_pos/cs_ev_hgt/cs_ev_yaw/cs_ev_vel True), both in Docker from samples/sitl-docker with pymavlink 2.4.50. Only a stationary pose was streamed; no flight on vision was tested. --msg vpe not run.
shows: ENU/FLU pose => NED/FRD ODOMETRY or VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE for EKF3 / EKF2
key_result: [EKF3](README.md#ardupilot-arducopter-copter-463-sitl) and [EKF2](README.md#px4-v1170-sih-quadrotor) fused a stationary ODOMETRY pose; no flight on vision

title: Drone frame to orthophoto geolocalization with LightGlue
summary: Matches a nadir drone frame against a georeferenced satellite or orthophoto tile with SuperPoint + LightGlue, fits a MAGSAC homography with OpenCV, and maps the frame centre through the GeoTIFF geotransform to lat/lon. The geometry (affine geotransform, homography mapping, WGS84 UTM, haversine) is a stdlib module with unit tests; the pipeline points at UAV-VisLoc, VPAIR and University-1652 for imagery and at hloc / AnyLoc for retrieval over large maps.
verified: geo_math.py and 12 unit tests ran with python3.14.7 stdlib on 2026-11-06. geolocalize.py ran on 2026-11-06 with torch 2.15.0 (CPU), LightGlue git 5a650c4, opencv-python 5.0.0.93, rasterio 1.5.2 on Python 3.12.14 against synthetic pairs cut from one public OpenAerialMap orthophoto (Tbilisi, CC-BY 4.0): 0.04-0.21 m error for yaw 0/60/135 deg, tilt and 60-150 m priors; 30.7 m error with 162 inliers when 40% of the frame was nodata at the ortho edge; a frame from a different city gave no fix (5 inliers). Frame and map come from the same survey, so this is a pipeline/geometry check, not a cross-season or real-UAV result; UAV-VisLoc/VPAIR/University-1652 were not run.
shows: Nadir frame => orthophoto match (LightGlue, MAGSAC homography, GeoTIFF transform) => lat/lon; stdlib geometry module
key_result: [Synthetic pairs from one real ortho](README.md#run): 0.04-0.21 m; 30.67 m wrong fix accepted at the ortho edge

title: Large-area visual place recognition for lost-GNSS recovery (DINOv2 GeM / VLAD over a 49 km2 NAIP tile DB, chained to LightGlue fine matching)
summary: The coarse first stage that geoloc-license-clean lacks: no position prior, unknown heading. Builds a geo-referenced tile DB over 49 km2 of public-domain NAIP (Planetary Computer, 5 vintages 2015-2023) at 250 m and 100 m tile sizes, 8 rotations. Global descriptors from DINOv2 ViT-S/14 (Apache-2.0): CLS, GeM, AnyLoc-style hard VLAD (own implementation), plus a classic rotation-invariant ring-histogram baseline. Compares four rotation strategies (none, query TTA, rotation-augmented DB, rotation-averaged invariant descriptor). Reports recall@1/5/10 within 50/100/250 m, latency and index size per map-vintage gap, then chains top-5 retrieval into ALIKED+LightGlue fine matching with the inlier gate and compares with fine matching given a known prior. Real CC0 eBee frames (2016) are also run.
verified: Ran 2026-11-06 on Apple M2 Max (DINOv2 ViT-S/14 on MPS, LightGlue on CPU, torch 2.15.0, Python 3.12.14): download_data.py fetched 49 km2 of NAIP 2015/2017/2019/2021/2023 from Planetary Computer, 23 CC0 eBee frames and 3DEP heights; run_vpr.py built 250 m and 100 m tile DBs (18.5k / 19.3k tiles x 8 rotations, ~9 min each) and scored 150 synthetic queries per source year: same imagery R@1 within 50 m 0.77 and R@10 within 100 m 0.98 (gem/invariant8, 250 m tiles), 2-8 year vintage gap 0.18-0.29 / 0.48-0.73; rotation-averaged GeM matched or beat an 8x rotation-augmented DB at 1/8 the index size; classic ring histogram R@10 within 250 m <= 0.13. Real eBee frames vs 2023 DB: cls/invariant8 R@1 within 50 m 0.70-0.74 (23 frames in one park). run_chain.py (VPR top-5 => ALIKED+LightGlue, 25-inlier gate): synthetic 20/20 fixes (same imagery, 0.22 m median), 8/20 and 3/20 at 6 and 4 year gaps vs 20/20 and 12/20 with a known prior; real eBee 0/23 with 100 m windows, 1/23 (20 m) with 50 m windows; no wrong fix accepted. Tests: 23 unittest cases pass in the venv; with plain python3 12 pass and 11 skip (numpy/OpenCV/torch absent).
shows: Coarse first stage for a lost UAV: DINOv2 GeM / CLS / VLAD retrieval over a 49 km2 NAIP tile DB with no position prior and unknown heading, chained to ALIKED + LightGlue fine matching with an inlier gate
runtime: download 6-25 min per NAIP vintage; DB build ~9 min per tile size (M2 Max, MPS); chain 7-26 s per query (CPU matcher)
key_result: [Same imagery, 250 m tiles](README.md#retrieval-db-2023-250-m-tiles-queries-cut-from-the-same-2023-imagery): R@1 within 50 m 0.77, R@10 within 100 m 0.98 (gem/invariant8); 2-8 year map gap R@10 0.48-0.73; [real 2016 eBee frames](README.md#real-ebee-frames-2016-vs-dbs-of-each-vintage) R@1 within 50 m 0.70-0.74, but the [fine stage](README.md#chain-vpr-top-5--fine-matching--inlier-gate-vs-fine-matching-with-a-known-prior) fixed only 1 of 23; no wrong fix accepted

name: Export control and ethics

If your project involves controlled hardware, non-public technical data, a defense customer, foreign team members on non-public work, or any RF transmission, ask your organisation's export-control or legal office, or the relevant authority, before you act. name: Hackathon playbook: navigation and PNT under GNSS denial
summary: For a team going into a navigation-themed hackathon that may have a military or defense track. Everything here is framed as defensive: keeping position, navigation and timing trustworthy, detecting interference, and giving operators an honest picture. Weapon terminal guidance and targeting are out of scope (see DoDD 3000.09 for where that line sits, and Policy, export control and ethics).

name: Learning paths
summary: Three study tracks built from the courses, talks, books and docs in this index. Pick one by how much time you have before the hackathon.

name: Model weights licenses: code vs weights vs training data
summary: Learned models in navigation pipelines carry three separate sets of terms:

name: 1. PNT fundamentals
summary: After this chapter you can describe any navigation system as "a state, an uncertainty, a set of measurements and a way to check they agree", and you will know the vocabulary judges use when they ask whether your solution is "assured".

name: 2. GNSS and its threats
summary: After this chapter you can explain how a receiver turns satellite signals into a position, read raw receiver output, pick between SPP, RTK and PPP, and build a jamming or spoofing detector that runs on recorded data.

name: 3. Inertial navigation and sensor fusion
summary: After this chapter you can explain why an IMU drifts, write the predict/update loop of a Kalman filter, choose between a filter and a factor graph, and configure an off-the-shelf estimator to survive a GNSS outage.

name: 4. Vision, LiDAR and radar odometry
summary: After this chapter you can explain how a camera, LiDAR or radar measures motion, what SLAM adds on top of odometry, and which open stack to run on which sensor. These are relative sources: they slow drift, they do not remove it. Absolute fixes are chapter 5.

name: 5. Absolute alternative PNT
summary: After this chapter you can explain the five main ways to get an absolute position without GNSS - image-to-map matching, terrain matching, magnetic anomaly matching, celestial fixes and signals of opportunity - pick the one that fits your platform, and feed its output into a filter as a measurement with honest uncertainty.

name: 6. Autopilots and C2
summary: After this chapter you can run PX4 or ArduPilot in simulation, inject your own position source over MAVLink, configure the estimator to switch away from GNSS, and push your vehicle's position and detections onto a TAK common operating picture.

name: 7. Maps, geodesy and planning
summary: After this chapter you can convert between the coordinate systems your tools disagree on, fetch free imagery and elevation data for a region, display it, and plan a path or a multi-vehicle mission over it.

name: 8. Maritime, underwater, ground and dismounted
summary: After this chapter you know how navigation changes off the drone: what ships broadcast and how spoofing shows up in it, how vehicles navigate underwater where no radio reaches, how ground robots and pedestrians dead-reckon, and which open stacks cover each domain.

name: 9. Evaluation and datasets
summary: After this chapter you can pick a dataset or simulator that matches your scenario, compute the trajectory metrics judges and reviewers expect, and design a GNSS-outage or interference test that shows what your system does when it matters.

name: Navigation primer
summary: A field guide to navigation and PNT (positioning, navigation and timing) for software engineers joining a defense-flavoured hackathon. Each chapter explains one cluster of the hub in plain language, names the ways it fails under electronic warfare (EW), and ends with two lists:

name: Problem-statement decoder
summary: Plausible problem statements for a navigation / PNT / GNSS-denied hackathon, each mapped to a recommended approach, a stack (integration cards first, catalog pages otherwise), datasets, a sample or template to start from, the main risk and a one-line pitch. Use it in the first 20 minutes of day 0: match the real statement to one to three rows, then score them with the rubric there.

name: Reference stacks: if you only have X, use Y
summary: Opinionated picks for a 24-48h build. One default per capability, one alternative, and what to avoid with the reason. "Avoid" means avoid under hackathon time pressure, not that the project is bad. Reasons come from each repo's catalog page (hackathon notes, maturity, archive status). Check the page for install lines before the event.

name: Timing resilience: the T in PNT
summary: After this page you can explain why a GNSS-denied system loses time before it loses position, estimate how long a given oscillator holds time from its datasheet, name the attacks on GNSS and network time, and pick a 24-48 h build that shows timing resilience with numbers.

name: Upstream findings
summary: Defects and gaps that the hub's samples found in other people's code and data, with what a maintainer needs to act on them. Nothing here has been reported. Every entry waits for the hub owner to decide whether, where and as whom to file it.
